tagline: An abandoned railroad grade carries the drive between limestone canyon walls.
intro: US 14A winds through a deep, narrow gorge carved by Spearfish Creek, linking Spearfish with Cheyenne Crossing. Limestone walls frame the road, and the Forest Service highlights Bridal Veil, Little Spearfish and Roughlock Falls as reasons to take this byway. The agency also recommends it for September color when the aspens change. The canyon’s vegetation brings together plants from the Rocky Mountains, eastern woodlands, northern forests and Great Plains.

The road follows a railway grade abandoned after massive flooding in 1933. Savoy and Elmore belonged to that earlier landscape of rail stops and mining camps. At the far end, Cheyenne Crossing recalls another transport system: in 1877 its stage station was the last of eleven stops on the Cheyenne to Deadwood route. That service ended in 1887, leaving the stables abandoned. Henry Fosha kept horses and supplies at the stage station before the railway grade became today’s driving route.

Begin at Spearfish, the town at the canyon’s mouth, and follow US 14A toward Cheyenne Crossing. Bridal Veil lies in a canyon section where mountain goats are commonly seen. Roughlock Falls Nature Area sits west of the byway near Little Spearfish Creek’s junction with Spearfish Creek. The drive finishes at Cheyenne Crossing, where the Lawrence County Historical Society erected a marker in 2024.
notice: Limestone canyon walls frame a road following the old railway grade.

moments.title: Bridal Veil Falls
moments.text: Bridal Veil is one of the waterfalls the Forest Service singles out along the canyon byway. This section of Spearfish Canyon is also a place where mountain goats are commonly seen. They were introduced into the Black Hills in the 1920s.

moments.title: Roughlock Falls
moments.text: Roughlock Falls Nature Area lies just west of US 14A, near the meeting of Little Spearfish Creek and Spearfish Creek. Within Black Hills National Forest, it is managed by the South Dakota Department of Game, Fish, and Parks. Hiking, fishing and birdwatching are among the activities here. The Forest Service includes Roughlock among the waterfalls that distinguish the canyon drive.

moments.title: Cheyenne Crossing
moments.text: Fresh horses once marked the last stage of the journey to Deadwood here. In 1877, Ice Box Canyon Valley Station was the final stop on an eleven-station route from Cheyenne. Henry Fosha operated the stable and barn, with a supply store across the dirt road. The station eventually took the name Cheyenne Crossing, replacing its earlier Ice Box Canyon Valley Station name. The stage service ended in 1887 and the stables were abandoned. Highway widening in the 1950s prompted the store’s relocation. A Lawrence County Historical Society marker, erected in 2024, marks this transport history on Spearfish Canyon Road.
